exam: A 25‑year‑old man presents with fever, new holosystolic murmur, and splinter haemorrhages. What is the next step? — Obtain blood cultures and start empiric IV antibiotics for suspected infective endocarditis.
A patient with known RHD develops dyspnoea at rest. What is the first investigation? — Bedside echocardiography to assess valve function and ventricular size.

A 60‑year‑old woman with hypertension presents with chest pain but normal ECG. What should you consider? — Silent myocardial infarction; obtain troponin and consider coronary angiography if resources allow.
You suspect acute pulmonary oedema in a resource‑limited setting. Which drug is first line? — Furosemide IV; avoid NSAIDs due to renal risk.
A patient with heart failure is on ACE inhibitor but develops cough. What is the management? — Discontinue ACE inhibitor and switch to an angiotensin receptor blocker.
A child with fever and a new diastolic rumble is found to have a normal chest X‑ray. What is the likely diagnosis? — Rheumatic mitral stenosis; confirm with echo.
A patient with HIV presents with fatigue and chest pain. Which cardiac complication is most common? — HIV‑associated cardiomyopathy; assess with echo and start ACE inhibitor.
A patient with suspected pericardial effusion has a normal ECG. What is the next step? — Perform bedside echocardiography to detect tamponade physiology.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Clinicians must integrate history, exam and limited tests to diagnose common cardiac diseases in East Africa. Focus on rheumatic heart disease, infective endocarditis, and cardiomyopathies.

b: Heart failure, arrhythmia, valvular disease, coronary disease
sections.p: Cardiovascular pathology refers to structural or functional abnormalities of the heart and vessels that impair haemodynamics. Diagnosis combines clinical clues with basic investigations such as ECG, chest X‑ray, and bedside echo when available.

t.b: Detects arrhythmias, ischemia, chamber enlargement – a Q wave suggests infarction; ST elevation >1 mm in two contiguous leads indicates acute MI.
Shows cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion, or pericardial effusion – a cardiothoracic ratio >0.55 suggests left ventricular enlargement.
Assesses valve morphology, ejection fraction, and pericardial fluid – a fractional shortening <25% indicates systolic dysfunction.
Hypertension is defined as systolic ≥140 mmHg or diastolic ≥90 mmHg; persistent elevation raises risk of stroke and heart failure.

b: NYHA I: no limitation; NYHA IV: symptoms at rest
sections.p: Staging uses clinical criteria and imaging. For heart failure, the New York Heart Association (NYHA) class I–IV guides therapy. Valvular disease severity is graded by valve area and pressure gradients.

t.b: EF <40% indicates severe systolic dysfunction; EF 40–55% is moderate; >55% is normal.

sections.p: In East Africa, rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains the leading cause of valvular disease. Infective endocarditis follows, often from dental or skin infections. Cardiomyopathies arise from malnutrition, HIV, and malaria.

t.b: Positive culture confirms recent infection; a negative result does not exclude RHD.
Positive for S. aureus or viridans streptococci supports endocarditis diagnosis.

b: Murmur: harsh holosystolic at apex suggests MR; diastolic rumble at apex indicates MS
sections.p: Patients may report dyspnoea, orthopnoea, palpitations, or chest pain. Physical signs include murmurs, displaced apex beat, jugular venous distension, and peripheral oedema.

t.b: Grade 1–6; a grade 4 murmur is usually clinically significant.

sections.p: Prioritise tests that are affordable and informative. When advanced imaging is unavailable, rely on ECG, chest X‑ray, and bedside echo.

t.b: Identifies arrhythmias and ischemia; a prolonged QT >440 ms signals risk of torsades.
Detects cardiomegaly; a cardiothoracic ratio >0.55 suggests LV enlargement.
Assesses valve function; a peak gradient >40 mmHg across a valve indicates severe stenosis.

b: Chest pain + ST elevation – acute MI
sections.p: Urgent signs include chest pain with ST elevation, sudden dyspnoea, syncope, or haemodynamic instability. Complications of untreated RHD include heart failure and thromboembolism.

b: Antibiotics – penicillin G for RHD prophylaxis; ceftriaxone for endocarditis
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first: antibiotics for endocarditis, anti‑tubercular therapy for TB pericarditis. Supportive care includes diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and anticoagulation where indicated.

t.b: Furosemide reduces pulmonary congestion; avoid NSAIDs due to renal risk.
Enalapril improves survival in systolic heart failure; monitor potassium.

sections.p: Regular review of cardiac status, adherence to secondary prophylaxis for RHD, and monitoring of drug side effects. Vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza reduces infection risk.

t.b: Repeat every 6–12 months to assess valve progression.
